items.prompt: A sync request is pending when the user logs out and signs back into the SAME account. Why is a user-id check alone not enough to discard the old response?
items.answer: The user id matches again, but the request belongs to an abandoned session; only the generation, bumped on every setSession, tells them apart
distractors: Because the user id changes on every login, so the check always fails
Because access tokens are compared instead, and they are identical
It is enough - the server rejects requests from previous sessions
items.explanation: The coordinator increments generation on every setSession and captures it when sync is requested, so a same-identity re-login still invalidates old work.

items.prompt: sync() stores this.tail = operation.catch(() => undefined) but returns operation itself. What would break if it stored this.tail = operation?
items.answer: After one failed attempt every later sync() would chain onto a rejected promise, runOnce would never run, and syncing would silently stop until restart
distractors: Nothing - the caller would simply see the error twice
Concurrent syncs would run in parallel instead of serially
The caller would no longer receive rejections from failed syncs
items.explanation: Catching only on the internal tail keeps the queue alive while the caller still observes the failure.

items.prompt: The outbox holds 1,200 events when a sync starts. What does one runOnce send?
items.answer: The first 500 events (readOutbox().slice(0, 500)) with the active credentials
distractors: All 1,200 events in a single request
Events in pages of 500 until the outbox is empty, within one runOnce
Only events recorded since the previous successful sync
items.explanation: Each attempt reads at most five hundred outbox events; the rest wait for a later sync.

items.prompt: A push returns 401 after the user has already logged out. What does runOnce do?
items.answer: The generation check before refresh fails, so it returns without requesting new credentials for the abandoned account
distractors: It refreshes the token and retries, then discards the result
It rethrows the 401 to the caller as an ordinary failure
It clears the outbox because the session is gone
items.explanation: Checking before refresh (line 91) and after refresh (line 93) keeps a late 401 from restoring a logged-out session.

items.prompt: push rejects with a network error that has no status. What happens?
items.answer: The error is rethrown: only a 401 triggers a refresh, and nothing is committed or acknowledged
distractors: A refresh is attempted for any failure, then push retries once
The batch is acknowledged so the outbox does not grow forever
The coordinator retries the push with exponential backoff
items.explanation: Other failures propagate without pretending progress was committed.

items.prompt: push returns acknowledgedIds ["a", "c"] but only event a was in the sent batch; c was recorded while the request was pending. What gets deleted from the outbox?
items.answer: Only a - acknowledgements are intersected with the ids of the sent batch, so c stays queued for the next sync
distractors: Both a and c, because the server acknowledged them
Nothing - an acknowledgement for an unknown id aborts the commit
The whole outbox, since the server returned fresh progress
items.explanation: The acknowledgement boundary is narrower than clearing the outbox: only identifiers present in the sent batch may be removed.

items.prompt: Why can the intersection at sync.ts:100-101 never filter anything in production today?
items.answer: The production push adapter builds acknowledgedIds from the sent events themselves, so nothing outside the batch can arrive
distractors: Because the server never returns acknowledgements at all
Because the outbox is cleared before each push
Because TypeScript prevents unknown ids from reaching the filter
items.explanation: It is belt-and-braces for a future adapter that trusts a server-supplied id list; keep it and pin it with a test.

items.prompt: What replaced the original separate baseline write followed by outboxClear?
items.answer: commitSyncedProgress, which upserts the baseline and deletes only the acknowledged ids inside one SQLite transaction
distractors: A server-side endpoint that clears the outbox remotely
Two writes ordered so the outbox is cleared before the baseline is saved
An in-memory cache that is flushed to SQLite on app background
items.explanation: Writing baseline and deleting acknowledgements together means a crash cannot leave one without the other.

items.prompt: Why does onCommit receive a fresh readOutbox() instead of the array read before the request?
items.answer: Events recorded while the request was pending must stay visible; publishing the pre-request array would re-show acknowledged events or hide new ones
distractors: Because the pre-request array was mutated by push and is no longer valid
Because React requires a new array reference to re-render
Because readOutbox is cheaper than copying the old array
items.explanation: Publication re-reads storage after the commit so the displayed state matches what is actually queued.

items.prompt: A profile update (updateMe) returns after a token refresh happened mid-flight. How does applyUserUpdate avoid restoring the outdated access token?
items.answer: After the generation and account checks, it merges the returned user into the coordinator's current tokens rather than the captured ones
distractors: It refreshes the token again before saving the profile
It replaces the whole token set with the one captured when updateMe started
It drops the profile update whenever a refresh has occurred
items.explanation: { ...this.tokens, user } preserves newer credentials instead of rebuilding authentication from an old closure.

items.prompt: Deleting the generation half of the guard on sync.ts line 99 leaves all six coordinator tests green. Why?
items.answer: The tests only switch to a different user or to logged out, which the user-id half already catches; no test re-logs in as the same user
distractors: The generation check on line 80 makes line 99 redundant
The tests mock the coordinator, so line 99 never runs
Vitest skips assertions inside async callbacks by default
items.explanation: The case that needs the generation is described but untested; exercise 6's same-user test kills the mutation.

items.prompt: The server's /sync response lists some events as rejected. What does the app do with them?
items.answer: The push adapter acknowledges every sent id and ignores rejected, so those events are deleted from the outbox and never surfaced or logged
distractors: They stay in the outbox and are retried on every sync
They are shown to the user as a sync error banner
They are moved to a separate dead-letter table for review
items.explanation: Deleting poison rows may be fine, but it should be a visible decision rather than a silent side effect.

items.front: State the single ownership principle behind the generation checks, the adoption/logout ordering and applyUserUpdate (see runOnce, src/lib/sync.ts:79-82).
items.back: Asynchronous results may mutate local account state only while their issuing session remains active. Each request captures its generation; every commit point re-checks it, and logout/adoption invalidate old work (setSession) before replacing account data.

items.front: authAdoptionMode(current, next) in src/lib/sync.ts:14-20 returns guest, same-account or account-switch. What does the provider do for guest vs account-switch?
items.back: guest (current null): no wipe - guest outbox events are kept and synced under the new account. account-switch (a to b): wipe A's baseline and outbox before adopting B, so one account's events never sync as another's.

items.front: Review criteria for sync changes (atomic commit at src/lib/storage.ts:42-52): list the five conditions.
items.back: setSession invalidation before clearing account data; baseline write and ack deletion in one transaction; acks limited to the sent batch; publication re-reads storage; and each has a test that fails when the line is removed.

items.front: Finding F4: syncNow ends in .catch(() => {}) (src/lib/progress.tsx:87). What is the operational cost?
items.back: Nothing records why a sync failed. The only signal is pendingCount not decreasing, so auth, network and server failures are indistinguishable and invisible.
